title: Why Physical AI Is So Hard To Engineer
gist: Semiconductor Engineering surveys EDA, IP and chip vendors on why physical AI (autonomous machines that sense, decide and act) is hard to engineer, citing real-time predictability, modularity for long product lives and hardware/software co-design. It quotes market sizing of about EUR 430 billion by 2030 from PwC and rapid adoption data from Deloitte.

themes.theme: What physical AI is and how it differs

insights.claim: Synopsys' Anthony Matarazzo frames physical AI as the move from generative AI to agentic workflow orchestration to AI in the physical world, where being wrong has life-or-death consequences.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: Rising cost of error is why physical AI needs new verification and safety methods beyond software AI.

insights.claim: Renesas' Brad Rex argues physical AI is an engineering problem orthogonal to IoT: IoT connected and monitored things while physical AI lets machines perceive and act autonomously in unstructured environments, requiring more sensing, real-time compute, power management and safety per device.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: Silicon content per device rises, which supports higher chip value in robots and autonomous machines.
insights.quote: This is a completely orthogonal engineering problem

insights.claim: Mixel's Justin Endo says physical AI is often framed as a compute story but is really an imaging story, because every robot, drone and autonomous system comes down to cameras feeding an inference engine, and the mobile camera interface is becoming the robot's optic nerve.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: Image-sensor and MIPI-style interface IP may capture value alongside compute.
insights.quote: The mobile camera interface is becoming the robot’s optic nerve

insights.claim: Arteris' Ashley Stevens splits physical AI devices into those that can rely on a cloud connection, such as factory robot arms, and those that must run fully locally, such as vehicles, because cellular coverage is inadequate in many places.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: Edge-resident inference is mandatory for mobile autonomous systems, favouring on-device compute.
insights.quote: vehicles cannot rely on continuous connectivity, as there are many locations where cellular coverage is inadequate

insights.claim: PwC estimates the global physical AI market at about EUR 430 billion by 2030, and Deloitte found 58% of companies report at least limited physical AI use today, projected to rise to 80% within two years.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: Adoption survey and market sizing are third-party but forecast-based; actual shipments will lag.
insights.quote: PwC estimates the global physical AI market will reach ~€430 billion by 2030

insights.claim: Velaura AI's Sanjay Gupta says industry estimates point to a multi-trillion-dollar total addressable market over ten years across robotics, drones, industrial automation, logistics, healthcare and defense.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: A promoter-style TAM far above PwC's figure; treat with caution.
insights.quote: several point to a multi-trillion-dollar total addressable market over the next 10 years

insights.claim: Arm's Robert Day estimates manufacturing, logistics and transportation represent about a $200 billion annual compute opportunity in the 2030s.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: A chip-IP vendor's sizing for the compute slice of physical AI.
insights.quote: an estimated $200 billion annual compute opportunity in the 2030s

insights.claim: Renesas expects the clearest near-term uses in industrial and logistics settings, where humanoid and non-humanoid robots handle repetitive or physically demanding tasks in structured environments made attractive by labor shortages.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: Structured factory and warehouse settings are likely first revenue pools for physical AI chips.
insights.quote: where labor shortages make automation valuable, and the environment is structured enough to deploy safely today

insights.claim: Adoption will be uneven and driven by market pressure; Vinci's Satish Radhakrishnan expects slow growth in each category but many sectors growing in parallel, and says time-to-market will be slower because people are still learning.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: Expect a broad, staggered ramp rather than a single inflection.
insights.quote: Each category is going to be separate and see slow growth, but there will be many sectors growing in parallel

insights.claim: Synopsys' Matarazzo asks what will train physical AI, noting the Internet trained generative AI but that reality has rules, calling training and simulation the big open question.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: Data scarcity and simulation fidelity could gate physical AI progress, favouring digital-twin and simulation vendors.
insights.quote: We know that the Internet trained generative AI, but what’s going to train physical AI?

insights.claim: Cars, robots and drones have high initial cost and long lives, so physical AI systems will need updatable hardware, sensors and actuators, not only software and models; older autonomous vehicles cannot be retrofitted to newer camera sensors and techniques.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: Product architecture will shift to replaceable compute and sensor modules, changing refresh-cycle economics.
insights.quote: Cars, robots, and drones have much higher initial cost, and they are expected to last many years.

insights.claim: Radhakrishnan suggests customers may accept paying about 10% of the original cost every two or three years to update compute or sensors, with software updates continuing to refresh the product.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: A possible recurring hardware-upgrade revenue model for robotics and autonomous vehicles, offered as speculation.
insights.quote: People may be okay with paying 10% of the original cost every two or three years

insights.claim: Renesas designs for headroom rather than a fixed end state, with extra compute margin, scalable power architectures and modular subsystems, while Cadence's William Chen notes memory architecture, communication fabrics and interface choices set the practical limits of future expansion.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: Early infrastructure choices lock in upgradeability limits, favouring multi-die and standards-based interfaces.
insights.quote: we design for headroom rather than attempting to predict a fixed end state

insights.claim: Physical AI optimises for latency, power, reliability and safety rather than throughput and utilisation, and Cadence's William Chen says a correct answer delivered too late may be operationally equivalent to a wrong answer.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: Data-centre AI design metrics do not carry over; predictability becomes the primary target.
insights.quote: A correct answer delivered too late may be operationally equivalent to a wrong answer.

insights.claim: proteanTecs' Alex Burlak argues the biggest limitation for physical AI chips is predictability under real operating conditions, since a timing issue or degradation in one of a humanoid's many MCUs could make a joint respond unexpectedly or a sensor input arrive late.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: Silicon health monitoring and aging analytics become safety features, not just reliability extras.
insights.quote: the biggest limitation is predictability under real operating conditions

insights.claim: Real-time AI may no longer allow past simplifications such as avoiding cache memory because it makes response times unpredictable, making embedded real-time design more complex than before.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: Compute architectures need new ways to deliver determinism alongside AI throughput.
insights.quote: It may not be possible to make many of the simplifications used in the past

insights.claim: Multiple vendors argue physical AI is among the strongest cases for hardware/software co-design, because control-loop behaviour emerges from sensing, memory access, inference, communication and actuation together, so mechanical design and battery technology must also be solved concurrently.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: Vertical integration and system-level design capability become competitive advantages.
insights.quote: Physical AI arguably represents one of the strongest cases for hardware/software co-design

insights.claim: MediaTek's Sameer Sharma says latency and bandwidth limits require silicon that handles AI workloads at the edge, including acceleration for machine vision and object classification, with a software stack linking perception, navigation, decision-making and control.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: Edge AI accelerators with integrated software stacks are the product category for robots and drones.
insights.quote: these devices require silicon capable of handling AI workloads at the edge

insights.claim: The article's conclusion is that physical AI is not about faster chips or more capable models but about coordinating sensing, computation and actuation predictably, requiring new approaches to architecture, co-design and verification as machines become more autonomous and stay in service longer.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: Tooling for system-level verification is a likely growth area for EDA vendors.
insights.quote: The challenge is not simply building faster chips or more capable AI models.
